passage:
My little brother Dhruv came home from school with his shoelace untied and his face all crumpled. I'm Manoj, I'm twelve, and I know that face.
At dinner Papa asked, "How was the week?"
"The worst," Dhruv said. "I lost my pencil box on Monday. Ma'am scolded me on Wednesday. And today nobody picked me for kho-kho."
I reminded him he won the drawing prize on Tuesday. He'd been bouncing about it for hours.
"That doesn't count," he said. "Tomorrow will be bad too. I just know."
I don't know everything going on in his head. Maybe the kho-kho thing hurt more than he's saying. After dinner I asked if he wanted to play carrom. He shrugged, then came.

qa.q: What prize did Dhruv win on Tuesday?
qa.a: The drawing prize.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv say the drawing prize 'doesn't count'?
qa.a: He is upset after not being picked for kho-kho, so right now only the bad things feel real and the good ones seem not to matter.

qa.q: What could Papa or Manoj do the next day to help Dhruv?
qa.a: Once Dhruv is calmer, they could ask him for one good and one bad thing from the day, so the good bits get a chance to be remembered.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Dhruv's 'worst week'?
qa.a: Manoj remembers Dhruv bouncing about the prize, so to Manoj the week looks mixed, and the kho-kho hurt seems to be colouring everything.

grounding: An older sibling watches an upset younger brother list only the week's bad events and predict a bad tomorrow, forgetting a recent prize.

passage:
Monday. Mohit laughed when Divyansh slipped in the corridor, and Divyansh stopped speaking to him. At home he flung his bag down. "This whole week is rubbish. Tomorrow will be rubbish." He couldn't think of one nice thing, not even last Friday's samosa party.
Wednesday. Divyansh sat alone at lunch, sure the maths test would go wrong. It went fine, but he told Nani it was "probably bad."
Saturday. Mohit knocked on the door with a borrowed comic and a sorry. They sat on the steps reading. "Remember the samosa party?" Mohit said, and Divyansh laughed. Suddenly he remembered the sunny PT period and his gold star too. "Huh," he said. "It wasn't all rubbish."

qa.q: What did Mohit bring on Saturday?
qa.a: A borrowed comic and a sorry.

qa.q: Why couldn't Divyansh think of one nice thing on Monday?
qa.a: He was hurt and angry after Mohit laughed, and that sad mood let only bad memories come to mind.

qa.q: What could help Divyansh on a day like Monday?
qa.a: Waiting until he feels calmer, or looking for one good thing from the week, like the samosa party, before deciding the whole week is rubbish.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt hearing the test was 'probably bad'?
qa.a: Nani may have worried, not knowing the test went fine and that his mood was doing the talking.

grounding: Across several days, an upset child sees only bad memories and expects a bad tomorrow, until making up with a friend brings the good ones back.

passage:
Ankita, you've got a face like a rainy day. Let your grandpa tell you something.
When I was ten, in Goa, my best friend moved away to Mumbai. That evening my mother asked how school was. I told her everything was terrible: the teacher hated me, I'd failed my sums, and the monsoon had ruined football. "Tomorrow will be worse," I said.
My mother just said, "Francis, write down the whole week tonight. Good and bad." I sat with the paper, and slowly it came back: nine out of ten in sums. The teacher had let me ring the bell. We'd played football in the rain, laughing.
I was still sad about my friend. But the week wasn't what my sadness said it was.
Now. What happened today?

qa.q: Where did young Francis's best friend move?
qa.a: To Mumbai.

qa.q: Why did ten-year-old Francis think tomorrow would be worse?
qa.a: Sad about losing his friend, he could only recall bad things, so the future looked bad too.

qa.q: Why did his mother's idea help, and could Ankita use it?
qa.a: Writing down the good and the bad brought forgotten good moments back; Ankita could try the same with today.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Ankita might feel understood and less alone, and more ready to tell grandpa about today. 🙂

grounding: A grandfather recalls being a sad ten-year-old who remembered only a bad week and expected worse, until writing it all down showed the good parts.

passage: The rain had flooded the lane outside the school, and Kiran's father was stuck in traffic, so Kiran waited in the empty staff room with Salma aunty, the office helper. Kiran had not won the drawing prize that afternoon. Swinging both legs, Kiran listed everything: "On Monday I spilled milk. On Tuesday I forgot my homework. Today I lost. This whole week was the worst week." "And tomorrow?" Salma aunty asked. "Tomorrow will be bad too. It always is." Salma aunty passed over a biscuit. "Didn't you tell me on Wednesday that your class clapped for your rabbit drawing?" Kiran stopped chewing. "...Oh. Yes." "And yesterday you got to feed the fish." Kiran's legs slowed. Outside, a horn honked twice. "That's Papa!" Kiran grabbed the bag and ran.

qa.q: What did Kiran spill on Monday?
qa.a: Milk.

qa.q: Why did Kiran believe the whole week was the worst?
qa.a: Feeling upset about losing the prize made only the bad moments come to mind, so the good ones, like the rabbit drawing, seemed to disappear.

qa.q: What did Salma aunty do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gently reminded Kiran of good things from the same week, so Kiran could see that sadness had been choosing which memories showed up.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Salma aunty, stuck with an upset child in the rain?
qa.a: Salma aunty stayed patient and kind, sharing a biscuit and listening, even though it meant waiting late at school.

grounding: A child upset after losing a prize remembers only the bad parts of the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage: In their Andheri flat, Deepika, eight, pushed rice around her plate. Her friend had sat with someone else at lunch. "This week was horrible," she told Farida Khala, who had come over for dinner. "On Monday the bus was late. On Tuesday I got a sum wrong. Today nobody sat with me. Tomorrow will be horrible too." Farida Khala raised an eyebrow. "Nothing good at all?" Deepika shook her head firmly, lips tight. Her mother caught Farida Khala's eye and said nothing. Next morning, sunlight on the balcony, Deepika was humming while tying her shoes. "Khala, did I tell you I came first in the sack race on Wednesday?" Farida Khala laughed. "Last night that race didn't exist." Deepika frowned, puzzled. "It was there all along," she said slowly.

qa.q: What did Deepika win on Wednesday?
qa.a: She came first in the sack race.

qa.q: Why couldn't Deepika remember the sack race at dinner?
qa.a: She was hurt about lunch, and the sad mood made her mind pull up only bad moments, so the win did not come to mind at all.

qa.q: How could a grown-up help Deepika the next time she feels sure a whole week was bad?
qa.a: They could wait for a calmer moment, or gently ask about one good thing from each day, so the mood doesn't choose all her memories.

qa.q: How might Farida Khala see the change between dinner and the next morning?
qa.a: Farida Khala seems amused and a little struck by it, seeing how one hurt feeling at night had hidden a happy memory.

grounding: A child upset over lunch remembers only the bad parts of her week and expects tomorrow to be bad, until her mood lifts.
